Dataset title: National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)
Description: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), also known as The Nation's Report Card, is the largest ongoing, nationally representative assessment of education in the United States. # Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

20 U.S. Code § 9622 - National Assessment of Educational Progress

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next
(a) Establishment

The Commissioner for Education Statistics shall, with the advice of the Assessment Board established under section 9621 of this title, carry out, through grants, contracts, or cooperative agreements with one or more qualified organizations, or consortia thereof, a National Assessment of Educational Progress, which collectively refers to a national assessment, State assessments, and a long-term trend assessment in reading and mathematics.

(b) Purpose; State assessments
(1) Purpose

The purpose of this section is to provide, in a timely manner, a fair and accurate measurement of student academic achievement and reporting of trends in such achievement in reading, mathematics, and other subject matter as specified in this section.

(2) Measurement and reportingThe Commissioner for Education Statistics, in carrying out the measurement and reporting described in paragraph (1), shall—
(A)
use a random sampling process which is consistent with relevant, widely accepted professional assessment standards and that produces data that are representative on a national and regional basis;
(B)
conduct a national assessment and collect and report assessment data, including achievement data trends, in a valid and reliable manner on student academic achievement in public and private elementary schools and secondary schools at least once every 2 years, in grades 4 and 8 in reading and mathematics;
(C)
conduct a national assessment and collect and report assessment data, including achievement data trends, in a valid and reliable manner on student academic achievement in public and private schools in reading and mathematics in grade 12 in regularly scheduled intervals, but at least as often as such assessments were conducted prior to January 8, 2002;
(D)
to the extent time and resources allow, and after the requirements described in subparagraph (B) are implemented and the requirements described in subparagraph (C) are met, conduct additional national assessments and collect and report assessment data, including achievement data trends, in a valid and reliable manner on student academic achievement in grades 4, 8, and 12 in public and private elementary schools and secondary schools in regularly scheduled intervals in additional subject matter, including writing, science, history, geography, civics, economics, foreign languages, and arts, and the trend assessment described in subparagraph (F);
(E)
conduct the reading and mathematics assessments described in subparagraph (B) in the same year, and every other year thereafter, to provide for 1 year in which no such assessments are conducted in between each administration of such assessments;
(F)
continue to conduct the trend assessment of academic achievement at ages 9, 13, and 17 for the purpose of maintaining data on long-term trends in reading and mathematics;
(G)
include information on special groups, including, whenever feasible, information collected, cross tabulated, compared, and reported by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, gender, disability and limited English proficiency; and
(H)
ensure that achievement data are made available on a timely basis following official reporting, in a manner that facilitates further analysis and that includes trend lines.
(3) State assessments
(A) In generalThe Commissioner for Education Statistics—
(i)
shall conduct biennial State academic assessments of student achievement in reading and mathematics in grades 4 and 8 as described in paragraphs (2)(B) and (2)(E);
(ii)
may conduct the State academic assessments of student achievement in reading and mathematics in grade 12 as described in paragraph (2)(C);
(iii)
may conduct State academic assessments of student achievement in grades 4, 8, and 12 as described in paragraph (2)(D); and
(iv)
shall conduct each such State assessment, in each subject area and at each grade level, on a developmental basis until the Commissioner for Education Statistics determines, as the result of an evaluation required by subsection (f), that such assessment produces high quality data that are valid and reliable.
(B) Agreement
(i) In general

States participating in State assessments shall enter into an agreement with the Secretary pursuant to subsection (d)(3).

(ii) Content

Such agreement shall contain information sufficient to give States full information about the process for decision-making (which shall include the consensus process used), on objectives to be tested, and the standards for random sampling, test administration, test security, data collection, validation, and reporting.

(C) Review and release
(i) In general

Except as provided in clause (ii), a participating State shall review and give permission for the release of results from any test of its students administered as a part of a State assessment prior to the release of such data. Refusal by a State to release its data shall not restrict the release of data from other States that have approved the release of such data.

(ii) Special rule

A State participating in the biennial academic assessments of student achievement in reading and mathematics in grades 4 and 8 shall be deemed to have given its permission to release its data if the State has an approved plan under section 6311 of this title.

(4) Prohibited activities
(A) In general

The use of assessment items and data on any assessment authorized under this section by an agent or agents of the Federal Government to rank, compare, or otherwise evaluate individual students or teachers, or to provide rewards or sanctions for individual students, teachers, schools or local educational agencies is prohibited.

(B) Special rule

Any assessment authorized under this section shall not be used by an agent or agents of the Federal Government to establish, require, or influence the standards, assessments, curriculum, including lesson plans, textbooks, or classroom materials, or instructional practices of States or local educational agencies.

(C) Applicability to student educational decisions

Nothing in this section shall be construed to prescribe the use of any assessment authorized under this section for student promotion or graduation purposes.

(D) Applicability to home schools

Nothing in this section shall be construed to affect home schools, whether or not a home school is treated as a home school or a private school under State law, nor shall any home schooled student be required to participate in any assessment referenced or authorized under this section.

(5) RequirementIn carrying out any assessment authorized under this section, the Commissioner for Education Statistics, in a manner consistent with subsection (c)(3), shall—
(A)
use widely accepted professional testing standards, objectively measure academic achievement, knowledge, and skills, and ensure that any academic assessment authorized under this section be tests that do not evaluate or assess personal or family beliefs and attitudes or publicly disclose personally identifiable information;
(B)
only collect information that is directly related to the appraisal of academic achievement, and to the fair and accurate presentation of such information; and
(C)
collect information on race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, disability, limited English proficiency, and gender.
(6) Technical assistance

In carrying out any assessment authorized under this section, the Commissioner for Education Statistics may provide technical assistance to States, localities, and other parties.

(c) Access
(1) Public access
(A) In general

Except as provided in paragraph (3), parents and members of the public shall have access to all assessment data, questions, and complete and current assessment instruments of any assessment authorized under this section. The local educational agency shal

​​​​​​​​​​​​NAEP Data Service API

Are you interested in obtaining NAEP results in a machine-readable format? Do you create your own data visualizations or use tools for data analytics?

The ins​​truction​​​​s below will help you to directly query the NAEP Data Service API to acquire JSON of the same results available in the NAEP Data​ Explorer.

Data service timeouts may occur when calls require too much time to complete. To avoid this, break up your calls into small manageable parts instead of large individual calls that span across multiple years. Data service results are not intended to be stored in spreadsheets or databases because these results may change over time​ and consequently may reflect inaccurate data.

If you ​​would like to report an issue or provide a suggestion for improving this API, please contact us.

Tab​le of Contents

  • The Basics
  • Request Types and Their Returns
  • Examples of Request Types and Their Returns
  • Parameter Values
  • Special and Optional Parameter Values​
  • Assessment Year and Subject Combinations
  • Error Codes

The Basics

Location/Path 

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/DataService/GetAdhocData.aspx

Response Format 

{"status":200,"result":[<1st result>, <2nd result>, …]}

  • If the request returns a successful response, status is 200.
  • A successful response will have a result that is an array.
  • Depending on the request, the result array may have more than 1 element.
Gaps
  • Gaps in the return are the score or percentage differences in NAEP results between different student groups, jurisdictions, or assessment years.
  • Gaps in the return can also mean differences in other previously calculated differences as mentioned above.

Back to Top

Request Types and Their Returns

Overview

  • Main URL – nationsreportcard.gov
  • Query String Parameters ​
    • Type – what kind of data to return
    • Subject – e.g., mathematics or reading
    • Grade – e.g., grades 4, 8, and 12
    • Subscale – For example, in addition to the composite mathematics scale (MRPCM), NAEP mathematics has five subscales, which are MRPS1: Numbers and Operations, MRPS2: Mathematics Measurement, MRPS3: Mathematics Geometry, MRPS4: Mathematics Data Analysis, Statistics, and Probability, MRPS: Mathematics Algebra and Functions.
    • Variable – student demographic groups (e.g., GENDER) or survey question variable or index.
    • ComparisonValues – allow you to choose specific variable categories (e.g., for GENDER, 1 is male and 2 is female)
    • Jurisdiction – national, state, and district 
    • Stattype – different type of statistical estimates (e.g. mean or percentages)
    • Year
    • StackType
      • Values
        • ColThenRow (default)
        • RowThenCol
      • Determines the order of returns
      • ColThenRow will group the returns based on the first variable (e.g. for SDRACE+GENDER, the return will be group by white+male, white+female, black+male, black+male …
      • RowThenCol will group the returns based on the second variable (e.g. for SDRACE+GENDER, the return will be group by white+male, black+male, hispanic+male, asian+male …
  • There are many data points. Each data point also contains the query information. For example, if you select 2 years, 1 jurisdiction, TOTAL (all students) and a composite scale, you will get 2 data points.  Each data point contains information indicating the year that the data point represents.
  • Please see the section Parameter Values below for more details for all parameters.
  • Significance indicates if the focal value is significantly higher or lower, or not significantly different than the target value.

Examples of Request Types and Their Returns

Basic data requests

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=data&subject=writing&grade=8&subscale=WRIRP&variable=GENDER&jurisdiction=NP&stattype=MN:MN&Year=2011
  • type – data​
  • Important return: value – the statistic you are looking for.

Crosstabluation data requests

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=data&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=SDRACE%2BGENDER&categoryindex=2%2B1,2%2B2,3%2B1,3%2B2&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2013,2015&StackType=RowThenCol
  • type – data
  • StackType
    • ColThenRow (default)
    • RowThenCol
  • Must have 2 variables (here is SDRACE and GENDER)
  • Important return : varValue – the category value within each student group  (e.g., for GENDER, male is 1, female is 2)

Significance gap across years

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=sigacrossyear&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=TOTAL&jurisdiction=NP&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015,2013
  • type – sigacrossyear
  • Used to return whether there is a significant difference in values between two or more years. The example shown here will return the comparison results between assessment years 2013 and 2015 in the average mathematics scores for public school students in the nation (NP).
  • Must have more than one year, separated by commas
  • Important returns 
    • focalValue – value for focal year
    • targetValue – value for target year
    • gap – difference between focalValue and targetValue

Significance gap across jurisdictions

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=sigacrossjuris&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=GENDER&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015,2013
  • Type – sigacrossjuris
  • Must have more than 1 jurisdiction, separated by commas
  • Important returns 
    • focalValue – value for a focal jurisdiction
    • targetValue – value for a target jurisdiction
    • gap – difference between focalValue and targetValue

Significance gap across variable

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=sigacrossvalue&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=GENDER&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015
  • Type – sigacrossvalue
  • Variable must be a non “TOTAL” value (e.g., GENDER in the example here)
  • Important returns
    • focalValue – value for variable focal category value (e.g. Male)
    • targetValue – value for variable target category value (e.g. Female)
    • gap – difference between focalValue and targetValue

Significance gap across variable (with crosstab)

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=sigacrossvalue&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=SDRACE%2BGENDER&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015
  • Type – sigacrossvalue
  • A crosstab will allow you to compare the relationship between two variables. You can examine the significance gap between specific demographic groups (e.g., (e.g., White/Male versus White/Female, White/Male versus Black/Male, etc.)
  • If the ComparisonValues parameter is not set, all variable categories from each variable will be compared to each other.
  • If the ComparisonValues parameter is set, you can return just the specific demographic groups you are interested in.
  • You may even choose up to three variables when performing crosstabs.

Gap between year and jurisdiction

 
https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=gaponyearacrossjuris&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=TOTAL&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015,2013
  • Type – gaponyearacrossjuris
  • Must have 2 years
  • Important returns
    • Innerdiff1 – difference between stattype values between 2 years for focal jurisdiction
    • Innerdiff2 – difference between stattype values between 2 years for target jurisdiction
    • Gap – difference between innerdiff1 and innerdiff2

Significance of gap of two variable category values across years

https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/Dataservice/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=gaponvaracrossyear&subject=mathematics&grade=8&subscale=MRPCM&variable=GENDER&jurisdiction=NP,CA&stattype=MN%3AMN&Year=2015,2013
  • Type – gaponvaracrossyear
  • Must have 2 or more years
  • Must have a non “TOTAL” variable with 2 or more category values (e.g. GENDER, SDRACE)
  • Important returns
    • Innerdiff1 – difference of stattype values between variable values (e.g., between male and female students) for focal year 
    • Innerdiff2 – difference of stattype values between variable values for target year

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)
Description: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), also known as The Nation's Report Card, is the largest ongoing, nationally representative assessment of education in the United States. Since 1969, NAEP has served as a vital measure of student achievement, providing valuable insights into academic performance and learning experiences across various subjects. Its results offer a comprehensive view of educational progress at the national level, across states, and in 27 urban districts.
URL: https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP)
## Research report for preservation, librarianship, analysis, and public policy

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Primary publisher:** National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), Institute of Education Sciences (IES), U.S. Department of Education  
**Official program website:** https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard  
**Official results website:** https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/

## Executive summary

**Your identification is correct, but NAEP is better understood as a continuing federal statistical and assessment program containing many datasets—not one downloadable dataset.** It includes achievement estimates, questionnaire results, restricted respondent-level files, assessment questions, technical documentation, and related studies.

Your description is substantially accurate, with three qualifications:

1. **The urban-district count is time-dependent.** The Governing Board’s overview cites **27 participating districts as of 2017**, while NCES’s district-program page lists **26 participating districts in 2024** and says 28 districts have participated over the program’s history. “27 urban districts” should therefore not be used as a timeless coverage statement.
2. **Coverage varies by assessment.** Not every subject, grade, year, or population has national, state, and district results.
3. **NAEP measures selected academic domains and learning experiences, not every aspect of educational progress.** It does not produce individual student or school report cards and does not, by itself, establish why achievement changed.

The strongest public benefit is a **common, relatively independent measure of achievement across jurisdictions and time**, supplementing state tests whose content and proficiency standards differ. Its greatest analytical hazards are confusing NAEP Proficient with grade-level proficiency, treating successive samples as a longitudinal student panel, ignoring survey-design uncertainty, and drawing causal conclusions from descriptive associations.

Sources: [NCES overview](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/), [Governing Board overview](https://www.nagb.gov/naep/about-naep.html), [NCES urban-district program](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tuda/).

---

## 1. Dataset identity and recommended catalog description

### Recommended description

> The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), known as The Nation’s Report Card, is a congressionally authorized, continuing assessment program administered by the National Center for Education Statistics. Beginning in 1969, it has measured achievement in selected academic subjects using representative samples of students. Main NAEP generally assesses grades 4, 8, and 12; a separate long-term trend program assesses age-defined populations. Depending on the assessment, results are available nationally, for states and other jurisdictions, and for participating urban school districts. Public products include aggregate achievement estimates, questionnaire results, released assessment questions, an interactive Data Explorer, a JSON API, reports, and technical documentation. Respondent-level research data generally require an NCES restricted-use license.

### Catalog essentials

| Field | Recommended entry or qualification |
|---|---|
| Preferred title | National Assessment of Educational Progress |
| Acronym / alternate title | NAEP / The Nation’s Report Card |
| Resource type | Continuing statistical program; collection of assessment datasets and publications |
| Corporate creator/publisher | U.S. Department of Education → IES → NCES |
| Policy-setting body | National Assessment Governing Board |
| Temporal coverage | Program begins in 1969; individual series have different starting dates |
| Geography | United States; participating states and jurisdictions; selected urban districts; separate Puerto Rico products |
| Population | Students enrolled in covered school populations and grades or ages, as defined for each assessment |
| Frequency | Assessment-specific; core grade 4/8 reading and mathematics generally biennial |
| Public access | Free aggregate results, reports, metadata, released items, and tools |
| Restricted access | Most respondent-level research files |
| Formats | HTML, JSON, Excel, PDF; public variable inventories also include CSV |
| Languages | Primarily English; Puerto Rico mathematics assessments and some resources involve Spanish |
| Identifier | Record assessment year, program, subject, grade/age, population, jurisdiction, and product identifier—not just “NAEP” |

**Cataloging recommendation:** Create a collection-level record plus assessment- or release-level records. A generic NAEP homepage URL cannot uniquely identify an analytical extract or establish which population it represents.

---

## 2. Who publishes, governs, and produces NAEP?

### NCES: statistical administration and publication

NCES administers NAEP under the leadership of the Commissioner for Education Statistics. It oversees operational work such as assessment development, sampling, administration, scoring, analysis, and reporting.

The two main federal websites have complementary roles:

- **nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard:** program information, methods, participation resources, research documentation, and access guidance.
- **nationsreportcard.gov:** interactive report cards, dashboards, Data Explorer, released questions, and data services.

### National Assessment Governing Board: policy

The Governing Board is an independent, bipartisan body established by law. Its responsibilities include assessment policy, frameworks, achievement levels, and the assessment schedule. Its membership includes public officials, educators, researchers, and members of the public.

**Important distinction:** The Board sets policy; NCES carries out the statistical program. They are not interchangeable publishers or custodians.

### Contractors and participating education agencies

The statute explicitly permits implementation through grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements. Historical NAEP production has relied on a contractor network, including:

- Educational Testing Service: assessment development, design, analysis, and reporting functions;
- Westat: sampling and field data collection;
- Pearson: processing and scoring;
- other contractors supporting technology, dissemination, coordination, and quality assurance.

These are documented historical roles, **not a verified list of all current 2026 contracts**. State coordinators, districts, schools, administrators, teachers, and sampled students also make collection possible.

Sources: [NCES governance](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/organization_governance.aspx), [authorizing statute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/9622), [historical NCES contract summaries](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/ies/document/2024/10/NCES%20awards.pdf).

---

## 3. Legal authority, mandate, and safeguards

### Core authority

The principal current statutory foundation is the **National Assessment of Educational Progress Authorization Act**, Title III of Public Law 107-279 (2002), codified primarily at:

- **20 U.S.C. § 9621:** National Assessment Governing Board;
- **20 U.S.C. § 9622:** NAEP administration, purposes, assessments, access, participation, and safeguards.

Section 9622 defines the purpose as timely, fair, and accurate measurement of academic achievement and reporting of trends.

Among its requirements are:

- representative random sampling consistent with accepted professional standards;
- national reading and mathematics assessments in grades 4 and 8 at least every two years;
- regularly scheduled grade 12 reading and mathematics assessments;
- biennial state reading and mathematics assessments in grades 4 and 8;
- continuation of long-term trend reading and mathematics assessments at ages 9, 13, and 17;
- additional subjects as time and resources allow;
- reporting for specified student groups when feasible;
- timely availability of achievement data for further analysis.

### Participation: mandatory at one level, voluntary at another

These distinctions matter:

- Under the No Child Left Behind Act and subsequently the Every Student Succeeds Act, **states receiving relevant federal aid must participate in grade 4/8 reading and mathematics NAEP**.
- Other state assessments are generally voluntary.
- Section 9622 states that participation is voluntary for **students, schools, and local educational agencies**.
- Parents must be informed that their child may be excused, need not finish, and need not answer any question.

State-level funding conditions should not be mistaken for compulsory student participation.

### Prohibited uses

The statute prohibits federal agents from using NAEP to:

- rank or evaluate individual students or teachers;
- provide rewards or sanctions for individual students, teachers, schools, or local education agencies;
- establish, require, or influence state or local standards, assessments, curriculum, textbooks, or instructional practices.

That last restriction concerns **federal use of NAEP to direct education**. It does not mean state officials, educators, or advocates cannot voluntarily learn from NAEP.

### Confidentiality

NAEP-specific protections in § 9622 are supplemented by **20 U.S.C. § 9573**, the IES confidentiality statute. These protect individually identifiable information and restrict its use to authorized research, statistical, or evaluation purposes.

Unauthorized disclosure or prohibited identification can carry criminal penalties. Confidentiality obligations are therefore substantive legal constraints, not merely website terms.

### Information-collection approval

NAEP collections also undergo Office of Management and Budget review under the Paperwork Reduction Act. Supporting statements are useful documentation of proposed collection design, respondent burden, costs, questionnaires, and changes between administrations.

Sources: [§ 9622](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/9622), [§ 9573](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A20+section%3A9573+edition%3Aprelim%29), [Board participation explanation](https://www.nagb.gov/naep/about-naep.html), [2026 collection supporting statement](https://omb.report/icr/202509-1850-001/doc/162942001.pdf).

---

## 4. History and development

NAEP arose from concern that national education statistics described educational **inputs**—enrollment, expenditures, facilities, and salaries—more thoroughly than what students actually knew.

| Period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| Early 1960s | Commissioner Francis Keppel promoted a technically sound national assessment of learning outcomes. |
| 1969 | First national assessments, including citizenship, science, and writing, assessed age-defined populations. |
| Early 1970s | Reading and mathematics series began that underpin today’s long-term trend reporting. |
| 1983–84 | Major redesign introduced item response theory, balanced incomplete-block assessment designs, and plausible values. |
| Mid-1980s onward | Main NAEP and long-term trend NAEP developed as distinct strands: updating assessments versus maintaining older trend measures. |
| 1988 | Congress established the independent Governing Board. |
| 1990 | State-level assessment began; achievement-level reporting and a new main mathematics trend series were introduced. |
| 1996 onward | Accommodation studies supported broader inclusion of students with disabilities and English learners. |
| 2002 | Urban-district assessments began after congressional funding; the current authorization statute was enacted. |
| 2003 onward | Required state participation strengthened the common grade 4/8 reading and mathematics series. |
| 2000s–2010s | Technology studies and digitally delivered assessments expanded. |
| 2017 | Major transition to digitally based main assessments, including reading and mathematics. |
| 2026 | Updated reading/mathematics frameworks and expanded use of school devices and internet require comparability studies. |

**Preservation implication:** “Since 1969” describes institutional continuity, not a single unchanged instrument or universally comparable series.

Sources: [NCES history](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/naephistory.aspx), [technical history](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/newnaephistory.aspx), [innovation timeline](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/about/timeline.aspx).

---

## 5. What data exist, and whom do they represent?

### Main NAEP

Main NAEP generally uses grade-based samples, especially grades **4, 8, and 12**. Subjects assessed over the program’s history include:

- mathematics and reading;
- science and writing;
- civics, U.S. history, and geography;
- arts and economics;
- technology and engineering literacy.

**This is a historical subject inventory, not a claim that each is currently assessed on a regular cycle.**

### Long-term trend NAEP

Long-term trend (LTT) is separate from main NAEP:

- age-based populations: traditionally ages **9, 13, and 17**;
- currently focused on reading and mathematics;
- designed to preserve long historical comparisons;
- different instruments and reporting conventions.

The **2025 LTT release covers ages 9 and 13**, not all three ages. It used paper-based assessments.

**Do not merge main and LTT scores into one trend line.**

### State and urban-district results

State results principally describe **public-school students** in the relevant grade and subject. National results may describe public and private students together or separately.

The urban-district program historically called **Trial Urban District Assessment (TUDA)** now appears on NCES pages as **Trends in Urban Districts Assessment**. It provides representative results within participating districts, principally at grades 4 and 8.

The participating districts are **not a probability sample of every urban district in America**. Their results cannot simply be averaged to represent all urban students.

District samples contribute to state and national samples with appropriate weighting. These overlapping populations matter for statistical comparisons.

### Other jurisdictions and population boundaries

Assessment-specific coverage can include the District of Columbia, Department of Defense Education Activity schools, and Bureau of Indian Education schools. Puerto Rico mathematics products require separate attention to language, sampling, and reporting definitions.

NAEP is principally a **school-enrollment-based assessment**, not a census of every child. Out-of-school youth, dropouts, and home-schooled populations are not comprehensively represented by ordinary main NAEP school samples. Grade 12 results describe students still enrolled in the covered population.

Sources: [2024 sample design](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tdw/sample_design/2024/naep_2024_sample_design.aspx), [TUDA](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tuda/), [2025 LTT design and results](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/ltt/2025/).

---

## 6. Contents and statistical design

### Main data components

| Component | Examples |
|---|---|
| Achievement estimates | Mean scale scores, percentiles, achievement-level percentages, subgroup gaps |
| Cognitive responses | Item responses and scored constructed responses in applicable research files |
| Student characteristics | Race/ethnicity, reported gender, disability status, English-learner status, socioeconomic indicators |
| Student questionnaires | Learning experiences, educational resources, subject-related activities |
| Teacher/school questionnaires | Instructional practices, school characteristics, resources, and context |
| Design variables | Student weights, replication information, assessment assignment, participation and accommodation information |
| Digital process data | Timing and interaction records for selected special products—not universally available |
| Interpretive materials | Frameworks, achievement-level descriptions, released questions, scoring rubrics, item maps |

Variable availability and wording change. A variable appearing in one assessment is not necessarily available or comparable in another.

### Why analysis is unusually demanding

NAEP combines:

1. **Complex probability sampling:** schools and students have unequal selection probabilities, with clustering, stratification, and nonresponse adjustments.
2. **Matrix sampling:** each student answers only part of the assessment item pool.
3. **Psychometric scaling:** item response theory places responses on assessment scales.
4. **Plausible values:** multiple draws represent uncertainty about achievement for population estimation.
5. **Replication-based variance estimation:** appropriate replicate weights and procedures estimate sampling uncertainty.

**Plausible values are not individual diagnostic scores.** Selecting one plausible value, or averaging a student’s plausible values and running ordinary unweighted analyses, does not reproduce appropriate NAEP inference.

Use all required plausible values and the assessment-specific survey design, combining uncertainty correctly.

NCES recommends software including **EdSurvey for R**, AM statistical software, and the legacy NAEP Data Toolkit. Some NCES software descriptions list older versions; verify current software support rather than treating the webpage’s version number as current.

Source: [NCES software guidance](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/researchcenter/software.aspx), [EdSurvey methodological overview](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/subject/researchcenter/pdf/edsurvey_overview.pdf).

---

## 7. Access routes, formats, and restrictions

### Public access

| Route | Best use | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| [NAEP Data Explorer](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/ndecore/) | Custom tables, charts, subgroup comparisons, significance and gap analyses | Aggregate estimates, not unrestricted raw records |
| [Data Service API](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/api_documentation.aspx) | Reproducible machine-readable retrieval | Live service; coverage and parameters must be checked |
| Report cards and dashboards | Accessible interpretation and public communication | Summarized presentation |
| [State/district snapshots](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/snapshots/) | Compact jurisdiction summaries | Less detailed than full tools |
| [Questions Tool](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/nqt/) | Released items, scoring guidance, performance information | Only released items, not the entire secure item bank |
| [Technical documentation](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tdw/) | Design, weighting, scaling, analysis, and quality evaluation | Must select the relevant assessment year |
| [Restricted-file variable inventories](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/researchcenter/variablesrudata.aspx) | Planning research and describing files | Metadata do not grant access to records |

The Data Explorer supports exports to Excel, Word, and PDF. NCES says most NAEP data from 1990 onward are available through it, but availability is product-specific.

### API

The documented endpoint is:

```text
https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/DataService/GetAdhocData.aspx
```

It returns JSON containing estimates and associated query information. Parameters specify subject, grade/cohort, scale, variables, jurisdiction, statistic, year, and program.

The documentation describes support for programs including main NDE, LTT, National Indian Education Study, school/teacher questionnaire products, and High School Transcript Study.

**Practical cautions:**

- Break large requests into smaller calls to avoid timeouts.
- Preserve variable and category lookup results.
- Specify actual years rather than moving aliases such as “Current.”
- Distinguish national public (`NP`) from national total (`NT`) populations.
- Preserve accommodation/sample suffixes where applicable: the documentation distinguishes `R2` and `R3`.
- Retrieve appropriate uncertainty information and flags.
- Check responses against official tables before building a pipeline.

The documentation contains inconsistent wording around optional standard-error parameters; test the current service rather than relying on a parameter name without validation.

### Restricted-use microdata

NCES describes respondent-level NAEP files, including weights, as available for secondary analysis after an organization obtains a restricted-use license. Its legacy pages describe CD-ROM delivery and availability beginning with 1990.

However, these pages also acknowledge incomplete metadata coverage for newer files. **Do not assume the legacy delivery medium, file inventory, or newest available assessment is current.** Confirm with NCES’s restricted-use program.

A library cannot lawfully turn a licensed microdata collection into a public repository merely because the aggregate results are public.

Sources: [available data for secondary analysis](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/researchcenter/datatools.aspx), [restricted-file inventories](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/researchcenter/variablesrudata.aspx), [API documentation](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/api_documentation.aspx).

---

## 8. Interpretation, quality, and common misuses

### Essential warnings

**1. NAEP Proficient does not mean “at grade level.”**  
It is a NAEP-specific performance standard reflecting competency over challenging material. Below Proficient does not automatically mean unable to read, failing, or below a state’s grade-level expectations.

**2. Achievement levels involve judgment.**  
Basic, Proficient, and Advanced are established through standard-setting. The statute provides for trial-basis use until the required validity determination; NCES technical documentation instructs users to interpret trial achievement levels cautiously.

**3. NAEP is not an individual longitudinal panel.**  
Successive assessments generally test different samples. A change among fourth-graders is not the measured growth of the same children.

**4. Associations are not causal effects.**  
Scores associated with homework, school type, resources, or questionnaire responses do not show what would happen if those factors were changed.

**5. Statistical uncertainty matters.**  
Small apparent changes or jurisdiction rankings may not be statistically distinguishable. “No significant change” is not proof of exact equality.

**6. Scales are not interchangeable.**  
A point in one subject, grade, or assessment series does not necessarily have the same meaning elsewhere. Do not convert score changes into “months of learning” without a separately justified model.

**7. Threshold percentages are incomplete summaries.**  
Percent Proficient can obscure changes below or above the cut point. Report means, percentiles, and achievement-level distributions where useful.

### Participation and exclusion

Exclusions, accommodations, absences, and nonresponse can affect comparisons. NCES publishes participation and inclusion information and conducts nonresponse-bias analyses when response rates fall below specified thresholds.

For 2024, several populations fell below the **85% threshold**, including private-school and BIE school samples and some grade 8 and grade 12 student samples. NCES’s analyses found no evidence of substantial residual student-nonresponse bias in the listed grade 8 jurisdictions after adjustments—but that is not a universal assurance for every population or variable.

### Demographic comparability

For subgroup work, check:

- changes in race/ethnicity classification;
- changes in English-learner and disability identification;
- changing accommodation policies;
- questionnaire wording and missingness;
- the meaning of free/reduced-price lunch eligibility, especially under changing school meal policies;
- district boundaries, school governance, and charter-school coverage.

Sources: [NCES interpretation guidance](https://www.nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/guides/), [achievement-level documentation](https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tdw/analysis/describing_achiev.aspx), [2024 nonresponse analyses](http://www.nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/tdw/weighting/2024/nonresponse_bias_analyses_for_the_2024_assessment.aspx), [independent National Academies review of interpretation](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/23409/chapter/8).

---

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

| User group | Typical use | Public benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Congress and federal agencies | Monitor national achievement and disparities | Evidence for oversight and public debate |
| State officials and legislatures | Compare trends using a common assessment | Context beyond differing state tests |
| Urban-district leaders | Compare district trends and student groups | Independent district-level benchmarking |
| Researchers and data scientists | Study achievement distributions, opportunity, and measurement | Reusable evidence and methodological research |
| Civil-rights and education advocates | Examine disparities and access to educational resources | Visibility for inequities hidden by averages |
| Teachers and curriculum specialists | Examine frameworks, released questions, and student work | Better understanding of assessed knowledge and skills |
| Journalists | Explain national and jurisdiction trends | Public access to comparable evidence |
| Parents and community organizations | Understand broad educational conditions | Accessible information without exposing children |
| Librarians and historians | Preserve evidence of learning and changing assessment policy | Long-term institutional memory |

### Why NAEP is particularly valuable

- **Common measurement:** states use different tests and proficiency standards.
- **Historical depth:** some series support comparisons spanning decades.
- **Distributional detail:** averages, percentiles, and subgroup estimates reveal different experiences.
- **Low stakes for individuals:** results are not used to grade participating students.
- **Public infrastructure:** free tools and an API reduce the cost of independent analysis.
- **Contextual information:** questionnaires document opportunities and experiences associated with achievement.

**Benefit does not equal proof of policy effectiveness.** NAEP can identify a problem, monitor a pattern, or test whether a claimed improvement is visible; it generally cannot establish that a particular law or instructional program caused the change.

---

## 10. Related studies and linkage opportunities

NAEP’s broader research environment includes:

- **National Indian Education Study:** achievement and educational experiences of American Indian and Alaska Native students;
- **High School Transcript Study:** course-taking and transcript information;
- **Oral Reading Fluency studies;**
- **digital process-data products;**
- **state proficiency mapping:** placing state proficiency standards in relation to NAEP scales;
- **NAEP–TIMSS linking studies;**
- **Puerto Rico mathematics studies;**
- **school and teacher questionnaire special studies.**

These have distinct designs and access conditions. They should not be treated as interchangeable extensions of a single student-level file.

Possible contextual sources include NCES school/district statistics, Census data, education-finance data, and state policy records.

**Linkage warning:** Public geography-level joins are not equivalent to authorized student or school linkage. Check population definitions, boundaries, dates, and license conditions. District of Columbia jurisdiction results and DC Public Schools district results are also different populations.

---

## 11. Current status and continuity considerations

### Recent releases and upcoming results

As checked in October 2026:

- Official sites provide **2024 main NAEP** reading and mathematics products, including grade 12, and grade 8 science.
- **2025 LTT reading and mathematics results for ages 9 and 13** were released in June 2026.
- The 2026 reading and mathematics assessments introduce updated frameworks and a transition toward school devices/internet.
- NCES’s 2026 planning explanation schedules reading/mathematics results for **early 2027**, with U.S. history and civics following in **summer 2027**. Release schedules remain subject to change.

The 2025 LTT results illustrate why distributions and assessment identity matter: nine-year-olds gained four points in both subjects relative to 2022, while thirteen-year-olds showed no statistically significant changes relative to 2023. These are LTT findings, not main NAEP state results.

Sources: [2025 LTT release](https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/ltt/2025/), [release announcement](https://www.nagb.gov/news-and-events/news-releases/2026/naep-long-term-trend-assessments-show-different-trends-for-9-and-13-year-olds.html), [2026 NCES planning explanation](https://ies.ed.gov/learn/blog/whats-horizon-2026-nations-report-card).

### Funding, cost, and governance risks

NAEP relies on federal appropriations, federal statistical expertise, contractor capacity, and school cooperation. Broader subject coverage is more resource-sensitive than the core mandated assessments.

An independent National Academies review identified substantial complexity in management and contracting and recommended an independent audit of management processes and costs. These findings are useful for policy oversight but are **historical estimates, not a current budget statement**.

I did not verify a final FY2026 enacted appropriation or a complete current contract roster. Those should be obtained from enacted appropriations, Department budget documents, and procurement records before making claims about current spending or institutional capacity.

Source: [National Academies, program management and costs](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/26427/chapter/12).

---

## 12. Preservation assessment and recommended strategy

### Overall assessment

**Preservation priority: high.** NAEP is an unusually valuable record of educational outcomes and measurement policy. Its statutory continuity helps, but legal authorization does not guarantee permanent accessibility of every historical interface, export, variable inventory, or technical document.

The following is a preservation recommendation, not a description of an existing NAEP archival policy.

### What to preserve

| Priority | Material | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | Official result tables with standard errors and footnotes | Core statistical evidence |
| Highest | Frameworks, scales, cut scores, achievement-level descriptions | Defines what the numbers mean |
| Highest | Sampling, weighting, scaling, linking, inclusion, and nonresponse documentation | Enables defensible interpretation |
| High | API responses, query URLs, parameter dictionaries, and code | Reproducibility |
| High | Questionnaires and variable inventories | Tracks changing constructs and categories |
| High | Released items, rubrics, exemplars, and item maps | Connects scores to assessed content |
| High | Calendars, correction notices, release announcements, and Board policy records | Documents provenance and change |
| Separate controlled collection | Licensed microdata and associated documentation | Valuable but legally restricted |

### Principal risks

1. **Dynamic interfaces:** a saved HTML page may not contain the data displayed by JavaScript.
2. **Live revisions:** API documentation warns that results may change.
3. **Distributed websites:** program, results, governance, software, and licensing records are spread across domains.
4. **Legacy delivery and software:** disc-based files and older extraction tools can become difficult to use.
5. **Incomplete metadata:** public inventories may lag newer restricted files.
6. **Semantic loss:** preserving values without populations, uncertainty, or sample definitions produces misleading data.
7. **Confidentiality:** public preservation cannot include unrestricted redistribution of licensed records.

### Recommended workflow

1. Define the preservation unit: program, subject, grade/age, assessment year, jurisdiction, population, and release.
2. Retain original downloads and raw JSON; create normalized CSV or columnar derivatives separately.
3. Capture rendered pages **and underlying data requests** where lawful.
4. Record retrieval time, complete URL/query, response status, checksums, software versions, and source footnotes.
5. Preserve codebooks, dictionaries, questionnaires, and technical documentation alongside extracts.
6. Keep immutable dated snapshots; compare later retrievals and document changes.
7. Validate selected values against official published tables.
8. Maintain a separate access-controlled process for restricted files under the license.
9. Deposit public materials in a durable repository with persistent identifiers and clear version labels.

**Important tension:** The API warns against storing results in spreadsheets or databases because they may become outdated. For preservation, the defensible response is to label saved outputs explicitly as **dated historical snapshots**, not as permanently current authoritative copies.

## 13. Rights, ethics, citation, and reproducibility

### Rights

Separate three issues:

- **Public statistics:** generally reusable factual information.
- **Federal-authored materials:** generally not subject to U.S. copyright under 17 U.S.C. § 105.
- **Third-party content, assessment passages, images, software, and licensed data:** may have separate rights or restrictions.

A `.gov` URL is not proof that every embedded object is public domain. I did not establish one blanket open license covering every NAEP artifact.

### Ethics

Responsible use should:

- avoid re-identification;
- avoid stigmatizing student groups;
- distinguish achievement differences from explanations of those differences;
- present uncertainty;
- use questionnaire-based socioeconomic indicators carefully;
- avoid calling below-Proficient students “illiterate” or “failing” without an independently appropriate measure.

### Recommended citation

For a public extract:

> U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Statistics. *National Assessment of Educational Progress: [program, subject, grade/age, assessment year, population and jurisdictions].* NAEP Data Explorer / Data Service API. Retrieved [date]. [Saved query or source URL]. [Repository identifier and snapshot version, if applicable].

For a publication, add its **NCES publication number**. For restricted data, follow the license and file documentation.

### Minimum reproducibility package

Include:

- research question and population definition;
- query URLs or extraction code;
- dated raw responses or permitted exports;
- variable and category dictionaries;
- all transformations;
- statistical methods;
- uncertainty estimates and suppression handling;
- relevant framework and technical-documentation references;
- software environment;
- explicit limitations.

---

## Bottom line

NAEP is **foundational public statistical infrastructure**, not an ordinary flat dataset. Its value comes from common assessment, representative sampling, historical continuity, and extensive documentation.

For the four perspectives in your request:

- **Preservationist:** preserve the evidence chain, not just charts or scores.
- **Data librarian:** catalog assessment-specific populations, versions, and access tiers.
- **Data scientist:** use survey-design and plausible-value methods; validate API extracts.
- **Policy activist:** use NAEP to document trends and disparities, while avoiding unsupported causal claims and misinterpretations of proficiency.

The most accurate short description replaces “27 urban districts” with **“participating urban districts, with coverage varying by assessment year”** and makes clear that public NAEP products are mainly population estimates, while detailed respondent-level research data are restricted.
